To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

children fail on the day-night task because of a combination of memory limitations and inhibitory deficits and that these limitations are overcome by a chunking strategy that reduces memory load and by a delay strategy that gives children time to inhibit a prepotently elicited response.
young children fail the day-night task when the response to be made is semantically related to and opposite of the response to be withheld.

children can hold two response rules in mind and can inhibit a response that is prepotent, but only when the task is simplified by removing the semantic relationship between correct response and to-be-inhibited prepotent response, by reducing the memory demand, and by allowing the child sufficient time.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the conditions under which 4- and 4 1.2-year-olds can hold two rules and inhibit a pre-potent response.
how children learn to control their responses to stimuli.
the development of cognitive processes that underlie children's ability to hold two rules in memory and inhibit a pre-potent response.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
young children are not able to inhibit a prepotant response if the correct response is semantically related to and is the opposite of the response to be withheld.
young children can hold 2 rules in mind and can inhibit saying what the picture depicts, but not if the to-be-activated and to-be-inhibited responses are semantically related and the direct opposite.
young children can inhibit a prepotant response if they can chunk the rules and if the to-be-included response is not semantically related to the to-be-inhibbited response.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
young children are not as bad at holding 2 rules in mind, inhibiting prepotent responses, or both, as we thought.
young children are not as good as older children at holding 2 rules in mind and at inhibiting prepotent responses.
young children can hold 2 rules in mind but have trouble inhibiting a prepotent but incorrect response.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the day-night task, and similar tasks, are not good measures of inhibitory control.
the day-night task is not a pure test of executive function.
young children can inhibit a prepotented response when the response to be suppressed is not related to the response to be made.
